## Appendix B Additional derivations of efficient influence functions

Here we work through the three-step outline presented following the statement of Theorem 2 in the main text to derive EIF’s in the models $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}$ , $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}$ , $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ , and $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}$ corresponding to examples 1, 2, 3, and 4.

### B.1 Restricted moment model

In the restricted moment model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}$ of Example 1, under suitable regularity conditions we have by standard $Z$ -estimation theory that the solution to

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}a(R_{i})(Y_{i}-\mu(R_{i};\beta))=0 $$

is a RAL estimator for $\beta\in\real^{q}$ for any $a\in\mathcal{H}_{R}^{q}$ . The corresponding influence function is

$$ \varphi_{0}(w;\beta^{*},\eta^{*})=\mathbb{E}\left[a(r)D(r;\beta^{*})^{\top}\right]^{-1}a(r)(y-\mu(r;\beta)) $$

where $D(r;b)=\mu_{\beta}(r;b)\equiv\partial\mu(r;\beta)/\partial\beta\Big|_{\beta=b}\in\real^{q}$ (cf. Chapter 5 of Van der Vaart (2000)). In the case that $\mu(r;\beta)=\psi(r)^{\top}\beta$ is a linear model, taking $a(r)=\psi(r)$ gives the ordinary least squares estimator. In any case, we can use $\varphi_{0}$ as above for our initial influence function of an RAL estimator of $\beta$ , which we aim to project via (7) to derive the EIF for $\beta$ in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}$ .

To do so, we first compute the semiparametric tangent space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}$ , similar to the example in Section 2.2. An arbitrary outcome mean function parametric submodel for $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ evidently takes the form

$$ m(r;\gamma)=\mu(r;\alpha(\gamma)) $$

for some smooth $\alpha:\real^{s}\rightarrow\real^{q}$ defined on a neighborhood of $0\in\real^{s}$ with $\alpha(0)=\beta^{*}$ . Then by the chain rule

$$ m_{\gamma}(r;0)=J_{\alpha}(0)^{\top}D(r;\beta^{*}) $$

for $J_{\alpha}(0)\in\real^{q\times s}$ a Jacobian matrix. For any $c_{0}\in\real^{s}$ , $c_{0}^{\top}m_{\gamma}(r;0)$ is of the form $r\mapsto c^{\top}D(r;\beta^{*})$ for some $c\in\real^{q}$ , which is evidently closed. Conversely, any function of this form clearly lies in the span of the derivative of the simple $q$ -dimensional submodel $m(r;\gamma)=\mu(r;\beta^{*}+\gamma)$ . It follows that

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}=\{r\mapsto c^{\top}D(r;\beta^{*})\mid c\in\real^{q}\}. $$

We note in passing that for the linear model $\mu(r;\beta)=\psi(r)^{\top}\beta$ we can verify that indeed $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}=\mathcal{M}_{1}$ , as shown by Proposition 2.

To derive the orthogonal complement $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\perp}$ , as suggested in Section 2.3 we solve for the set of functions $h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ for which the projection $g=\Pi(h;\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}})$ is equal to 0. We have $g(r)=c_{h}^{\top}D(r;\beta^{*})$ where

$$ c_{h}=\argmin_{c\in\real^{q}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(h(R)-c^{\top}D(R;\beta^{*})\right)^{2}\right] $$

Taking a derivative gives

$$ c_{h}=\left(\mathbb{E}[D(R;\beta^{*})D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]\right)^{-1}\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})] $$

so $g=0\iff c_{h}=0\iff\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})=0]$ . It follows that

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\perp}=\{h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}\mid\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})]=0\}. $$

and (by Theorem 2) that

$$ \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\perp}=\{w\mapsto h(r)(y-\mu(r;\beta^{*}))\mid\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})]=0\}. $$

Finally, we compute the projection $g=\Pi\left(\varphi_{0};\left(\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\perp}\right)^{q}\right)$ to get the EIF via (7). By definition, $g(w)=(y-\mu(r;\beta^{*}))h_{0}(r)$ where

$$ \displaystyle h_{0} \displaystyle=\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}^{q}:\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]=0}\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\mu(R;\beta^{*}))^{2}\|A^{-1}a(R)-h(X)\|^{2}\right] \displaystyle A \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[a(R)D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]. $$

To compute this projection, we handle the constraint $\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]=0$ by introducing a Lagrange multiplier $\Lambda\in\real^{q\times q}$ . Then we minimize the Lagrangian by conditioning on $R$ and minimizing pointwise:

$$ \displaystyle\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}^{q}}\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\mu(R;\beta^{*}))^{2}\|A^{-1}a(R)-h(R)\|^{2}\right]-2\textnormal{tr}\left(\Lambda^{\top}\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]\right) \displaystyle\quad=\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}^{q}}\mathbb{E}\left[V^{*}(R)\|h(R)\|^{2}-2\left(V^{*}(R)a(R)^{\top}A^{-1}+D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}\Lambda^{\top}\right)h(R)\right] $$

Minimizing the argument to the expectation pointwise gives

$$ h_{0}(r)=A^{-1}a(r)+\frac{1}{V^{*}(r)}\Lambda D(r;\beta^{*}) $$

We solve for the Lagrange multiplier $\Lambda$ by plugging the preceding display into the matrix equations $\mathbb{E}[h_{0}(R)D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]=0$ , giving

$$ \Lambda=-\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{V^{*}(R)}D(R;\beta^{*})D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}\right]\right)^{-1}. $$

Then the EIF is

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}(w;\beta^{*},\eta^{*}) \displaystyle=\varphi_{0}(w;\beta^{*},\eta^{*})-h_{0}(r)(y-\mu(r;\beta^{*})) \displaystyle=\frac{y-\mu(r;\beta^{*})}{V^{*}(r)}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{V^{*}(R)}D(R;\beta^{*})D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}\right]\right)^{-1}D(r;\beta^{*}) $$

which matches equation (4.55) of Tsiatis (2006).

### B.2 Mean-exchangeable controls

We derive EIF’s in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}$ . We can use $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}$ and $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}}$ as the initial influence functions $\varphi_{0}$ . By Proposition 2, we know $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}=\mathcal{M}_{2}$ . It only remains to compute $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp}$ and the projection (7).

As in the derivation of $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}^{\perp}$ in the main text, we characterize $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp}$ as the set of all functions $h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ for which $g=\Pi(h;\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}})=0$ . To that end we write $h(r)=zh_{11}(x)+(1-s)h_{01}(x)+s(1-z)h_{10}(x)$ and

$$ g=zg_{1}(x)+(1-z)g_{0}(x) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle(g_{0},g_{1}) \displaystyle=\argmin_{(f_{0},f_{1})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}^{2}}\mathbb{E}[(h(R)-Zf_{1}(X)-(1-Z)f_{0}(X))^{2}] \displaystyle=\argmin_{(f_{0},f_{1})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}^{2}}\mathbb{E}[Z(h_{11}(X)-f_{1}(X))^{2}] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[(1-S)(h_{01}(X)-f_{0}(X))^{2}+S(1-Z)(h_{10}(X)-f_{0}(X))^{2}] \displaystyle=\argmin_{(f_{0},f_{1})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}^{2}}\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(h_{11}(X)-f_{1}(X))^{2}+(1-p^{*}(X))(h_{01}(X)-f_{0}(X))^{2}] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))(h_{10}(X)-f_{0}(X))^{2}]. $$

The final equality follows by conditioning on $X$ , and expresses the objective as the expectation of a function of $X$ . Without any restrictions on $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$ we can perform the minimization by minimizing the argument of the expectation pointwise in $x$ . Writing the first order conditions, we find they are satisfied by $f_{0}=f_{1}=0$ if and only if

$$ \displaystyle p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)h_{11}(x) \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))h_{10}(x)+(1-p^{*}(x))h_{00}(x) \displaystyle=0 $$

for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ . Hence $h\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp}$ if and only if $h_{11}(x)=0$ and $h_{10}(x)=-\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}h_{00}(x)$ , with $h_{00}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ free to vary. In other words

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp}=\left\{r\mapsto\left[(1-s)-s(1-z)\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}\right]\zeta(x)\Big|\zeta\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\right\} $$

and so by Theorem 2

$$ \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp}=\left\{w\mapsto\left[(1-s)-s(1-z)\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}\right]\zeta(x)(y-m^{*}(r))\Big|\zeta\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\right\}. $$

Now we compute the projection $g=\Pi(\varphi_{0};\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp})$ from (7) in terms of $\varphi_{0}$ . We write

$$ g(w)=\left[(1-s)-s(1-z)\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}\right]\zeta(x)(y-m^{*}(r)) $$

where

$$ \zeta=\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}(W)-\left[(1-S)-S(1-Z)\frac{1-p^{*}(X)}{p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))}\right]h(X)(Y-m^{*}(R))\right)^{2}\right]. $$

By our usual approach of rewriting the objective as the expectation of a function of $X$ by iterated expectations and then minimizing the argument of this expectation pointwise, we get

$$ \zeta(x)=\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\varphi_{0}(W)\left((1-S)-S(1-Z)\frac{1-p^{*}(X)}{p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))}\right)(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid X=x\right]}{(1-p^{*}(x))V_{00}^{*}(x)+\frac{(1-p^{*}(x))^{2}}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}V_{10}^{*}(x)} $$

For $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}$ we observe

$$ \mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0}(W;\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*},\eta^{*})(1-S)(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid X]=0 $$

while

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[-\varphi_{0}(W;\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*},\eta^{*})S(1-Z)\frac{1-p^{*}(X)}{p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))}(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid X\right]=\frac{(1-p^{*}(X))^{2}V_{10}^{*}(X)}{p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))(1-\rho^{*})}. $$

Hence

$$ \zeta(x)=\frac{(1-p^{*}(x))V_{10}^{*}(x)}{(1-\rho^{*})[V_{00}^{*}(x)p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))+V_{10}^{*}(x)(1-p^{*}(x))]} $$

and then the EIF for $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ is

$$ \varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}(w;\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*},\eta^{*})=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}(w;\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*},\eta^{*})-\left[(1-s)-s(1-z)\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}\right]\zeta(x)(y-m^{*}(z,x)) $$

which after algebraic simplification matches the expression given in Proposition 3 of Li et al. (2023b).

Repeating the calculation in the preceding paragraph with $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}}$ gives the efficiency bound for $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ , also given in Proposition 3 of Li et al. (2023b).

### B.3 Parametric confounding bias and CATE

Following our three-step outline, we derive EIF’s in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ in terms of an arbitrary influence function $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0}(\cdot,\tau,\eta)$ for an RAL estimator of some generic pathwise-differentiable estimand $\tau$ . We later specialize to the estimand $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ using $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}$ , which verifies Theorem 4 of Yang et al. (2024).

We begin by deriving the outcome mean function tangent space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ . The method to do so is similar to that of Appendix B.1. In words, the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ allows the control level ( $z=0$ ) of the outcome mean function to be an arbitrary function of $(s,x)$ . Then given the control level, the treatment level differs by $\mu(x;\beta)$ from the control level when $s=1$ , and by $\mu(x;\beta)+\phi(x;\theta)$ from the control level when $s=0$ . Formalizing this mathematically, this means that an arbitrary outcome mean function parametric submodel of $\mathcal{M}_{3}$ must take the form

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:M_{3}{}_{s}ubmodel}m(r;\gamma)=f_{0}(s,x;\gamma_{0})+z[\mu(x;\beta(\gamma_{1}))+(1-s)\phi(x;\theta(\gamma_{2}))] $$

for some smooth mappings $\beta:\real^{s_{1}}\rightarrow\real^{p}$ and $\theta:\real^{s_{2}}\rightarrow\real^{q}$ , where $\gamma=(\gamma_{0}^{\top},\gamma_{1}^{\top},\gamma_{2}^{\top})^{\top}$ and $\gamma_{i}\in\real^{s_{i}}$ , $i=0,1,2$ . Then using the subscript notation for (partial) derivatives from Example 5 in Section 2 of the main text, for arbitrary $c=(c_{0}^{\top},c_{1}^{\top},c_{2}^{\top})^{\top}$ partitioned in the same way as $\gamma$ , we have

$$ c^{\top}m_{\gamma}(r;0)=c_{0}^{\top}f_{0}^{\prime}(s,x;0)+zc_{1}^{\top}J_{\beta}(0)^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+z(1-s)c_{2}^{\top}J_{\theta}(0)^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*}) $$

where $J_{\beta}(0)\in\real^{p\times s_{1}}$ and $J_{\theta}(0)\in\real^{q\times s_{2}}$ are the Jacobian matrices for the mappings $\beta$ and $\theta$ at 0, and

$$ D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})=\frac{\partial\mu(x;\beta)}{\partial\beta}\Big|_{\beta=\beta^{*}},\quad D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})=\frac{\partial\phi(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta}\Big|_{\theta=\theta^{*}}. $$

This is of the form

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:S_{M}{}_{3}{}_{f}orm}f(s,x)+z[c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+(1-s)c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})] $$

for some $f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ , $c_{1}\in\real^{p}$ , $c_{2}\in\real^{q}$ (note we have overloaded the notation for $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ ). Conversely, we now show that any function of the form (50), for some $f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ , $c_{1}\in\real^{p}$ , $c_{2}\in\real^{q}$ , lies in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ . To that end, consider the submodel of the form (49) with $s_{0}=1$ , $s_{1}=p$ , $s_{2}=q$ and $f(s,x)=m^{*}(s,0,x)+\gamma_{0}f(s,x)$ , $\beta(\gamma_{1})=\beta^{*}+\gamma_{1}$ , and $\theta(\gamma_{2})=\theta^{*}+\gamma_{2}$ . We observe that our function given by (50) is equivalent to $c^{\top}m_{\gamma}(r;0)$ for $c=(1,c_{1}^{\top},c_{2}^{\top})$ , and thus lies in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ by definition. We conclude that indeed,

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:S_{M}{}_{3}}\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}=\{r\mapsto f(s,x)+z[c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+(1-s)c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})]\mid f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX},c_{1}\in\real^{p},c_{2}\in\real^{q}\}. $$

It remains to compute the orthogonal complement $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp}$ and then the projection (7). As in the other examples, we compute $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp}$ as the set of all functions $h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ for which $g=\Pi(h;\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}})=0$ . Given $h$ we write

$$ g(r)=f_{0}(s,x)+z[d_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+(1-s)d_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})] $$

where

$$ (f_{0},d_{1},d_{2})=\argmin_{f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX},c_{1}\in\real^{p},c_{2}\in\real^{q}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(h(R)-f(S,X)-Z[c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})+(1-S)c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})]\right)^{2}\right]. $$

As we have seen, we can solve this minimization by rewriting the objective as the expectation of a function of solely $X$ via iterated expectations:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(h(R)-f(S,X)-Z[c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})+(1-S)c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})]\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(h_{11}(X)-f(1,X)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*}))^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))(h_{10}(X)-f(1,X))^{2}] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(h_{01}(X)-f(0,X)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})-c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*}))^{2}] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))(1-q^{*}(X))(h_{00}(X)-f(0,X))^{2}] $$

For fixed $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ , the minimizer of this objective in $f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ takes the form $f(s,x)=sf(1,x)+(1-s)f(0,x)$ where $f(1,x)$ and $f(0,x)$ globally minimize the argument to the expectation, i.e. they satisfy the first-order conditions

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(h_{11}(x)-f(1,x)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*}))+p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))(h_{10}(x)-f(1,x))^{2} \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)(h_{01}(x)-f(0,x)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})-c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})) \displaystyle\quad+(1-p^{*}(x))(1-q^{*}(x))(h_{00}(x)-f(0,x)) $$

Conversely for any fixed $f\in\mathcal{S}_{SX}$ , taking the derivative of the objective shows that the minimizers $c_{1}\in\real^{p}$ and $c_{2}\in\real^{q}$ must satisfy the first order conditions

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(h_{11}(X)-f_{1}(X)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*}))D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(h_{01}(X)-f(0,X)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})-c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*}))D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})] \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(h_{01}(X)-f(0,X)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})-c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*}))D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})] $$

The four first-order conditions are satisfied with $f(0,x)=f(1,x)=0$ and $c_{1}=c_{2}=0$ if and only if

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)h_{11}(X)+(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)h_{01}(X)]D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})] \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)h_{01}(X)D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})] \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle e^{*}(x)h_{11}(x)+(1-e^{*}(x))h_{10}(x) \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle q^{*}(x)h_{01}(x)+(1-q^{*}(x))h_{00}(x) \displaystyle=0. $$

Thus $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp}$ is the set of all functions $h$ satisfying (52), (53), (54), and (55). Recognizing that (54) and (55) determine $h_{00}$ and $h_{10}$ in terms of $h_{11}$ and $h_{01}$ , respectively, which are free to vary other than the moment constraints given by (52) and (53), we can compactly write $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp}$ as the set of all mappings

$$ r\mapsto f(s,x)\left[z-(1-z)\left(\frac{se^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}+\frac{(1-s)q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}\right)\right] $$

such that $f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ with

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)f(1,X)+(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)f(0,X))D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})] \displaystyle=0\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)f(1,X)D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})] \displaystyle=0. $$

Finally, we compute the projection (7). Given the initial influence function $\varphi_{0}$ , we have by the form of $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp}$ derived in the previous paragraph and Theorem 2 that

$$ \pi(\varphi_{0};\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp})=w\mapsto\left(s\Gamma_{1}^{*}(x)+(1-s)\Gamma_{0}^{*}(x)\right)\left(z-(1-z)\left[\frac{se^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}+\frac{(1-s)q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}\right]\right)(y-m^{*}(r)) $$

where $\Gamma_{0}^{*}$ and $\Gamma_{1}^{*}$ solve the optimization problem

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\Gamma_{0}\in\mathcal{H}_{X},\Gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-\left[S\Gamma_{1}(X)+(1-S)\Gamma_{0}(X)\right]\nu^{*}(R)\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)\Gamma_{1}(X)+(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)\Gamma_{0}(X)]D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})]=0,\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)\Gamma_{0}(X)D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})]=0 $$

with

$$ \nu^{*}(r)=\nu(r;\eta^{*})\text{ for }\nu(r;\eta)=\left[z-(1-z)\left(\frac{se^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}+\frac{(1-s)q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}\right)\right](y-m^{*}(r)). $$

Once again, we rewrite the objective by conditioning on $X$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-\left(S\Gamma_{1}(X)+(1-S)\Gamma_{0}(X)\right)\nu^{*}(R)\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})^{2}\mid X]+\mathbb{E}\left[\Gamma_{1}^{2}(X)p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)\left(V_{11}^{*}(X)+\frac{e^{*}(X)}{1-e^{*}(X)}V_{10}^{*}(X)\right)\right] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}\left[\Gamma_{0}^{2}(X)(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)\left(V_{01}^{*}(X)+\frac{q^{*}(X)}{1-q^{*}(X)}V_{00}^{*}(X)\right)\right]-2\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{J}(X;\Gamma_{0},\Gamma_{1},\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})] $$

where

$$ \mathcal{J}(x;\Gamma_{0},\Gamma_{1},\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(S\Gamma_{1}(X)+(1-S)\Gamma_{0}(X)\right)\nu^{*}(R)\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\mid X=x\right]. $$

To deal with the two moment constraints, we introduce Lagrange multipliers $\Lambda_{1}\in\real^{p}$ and $\Lambda_{2}\in\real^{q}$ , similar to Appendix B.1. Dropping the constant $\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})^{2}\mid X=x]$ term from the objective, the Lagrangian is $\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(X)]$ where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}(x) \displaystyle=\Gamma_{1}^{2}(x)p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)\left(V_{11}^{*}(x)+\frac{e^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}V_{10}^{*}(x)\right) \displaystyle\quad+\Gamma_{0}^{2}(x)(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)\left(V_{01}^{*}(x)+\frac{q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}V_{00}^{*}(x)\right) \displaystyle\quad-2\mathcal{J}(x;\Gamma_{0},\Gamma_{1},\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0}) \displaystyle\quad-2\Lambda_{1}^{\top}[p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)\Gamma_{1}(x)+(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)\Gamma_{0}(x)]D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*}) \displaystyle\quad-2\Lambda_{2}^{\top}[(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)\Gamma_{0}(x)D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})]. $$

We can minimize the Lagrangian over $\Gamma_{0}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ and $\Gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ by minimizing $\mathcal{L}(x)$ pointwise, giving

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma_{0}^{*}(x) \displaystyle=(1-q^{*}(x))\left(\frac{\Lambda_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+\Lambda_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})}{(1-q^{*}(x))V_{01}^{*}(x)+q^{*}(x)V_{00}^{*}(x)}\right) \displaystyle\quad+\frac{(1-q^{*}(x))\mathcal{J}_{0}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})}{(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)[(1-q^{*}(x))V_{01}^{*}(x)+q^{*}(x)V_{00}^{*}(x)]} \displaystyle\Gamma_{1}^{*}(x) \displaystyle=(1-e^{*}(x))\left(\frac{\Lambda_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})}{(1-e^{*}(x))V_{11}^{*}(x)+e^{*}(x)V_{10}^{*}(x)}\right) \displaystyle\quad+\frac{(1-e^{*}(x))\mathcal{J}_{1}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})}{p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)[(1-e^{*}(x))V_{11}^{*}(x)+e^{*}(x)V_{10}^{*}(x)]} $$

where the Lagrange multipliers can be solved for by plugging back into the moment constraints and

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{1}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[S\left(Z-(1-Z)\frac{e^{*}(X)}{1-e^{*}(X)}\right)(Y-m^{*}(R))\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\mid X=x\right] \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{0}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[(1-S)\left(Z-(1-Z)\frac{q^{*}(X)}{1-q^{*}(X)}\right)(Y-m^{*}(R))\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\mid X=x\right] $$

which come from writing

$$ \mathcal{J}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})=\mathcal{J}_{1}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})\Gamma_{1}(x)+\mathcal{J}_{1}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})\Gamma_{0}(x). $$

This shows that $\Lambda_{1}$ and $\Lambda_{2}$ solve the linear matrix system

$$ \displaystyle A_{\mu\mu}\Lambda_{1}+A_{\mu\phi}\Lambda_{2} \displaystyle=-b_{\mu} \displaystyle A_{\mu\phi}^{\top}+A_{\phi\phi}\Lambda_{2} \displaystyle=-b_{\phi} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle A_{\mu\mu} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))}{(1-e^{*}(X))V_{11}^{*}(X)+e^{*}(X)V_{10}^{*}(X)}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})^{\top}\right] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(1-q^{*}(X))}{(1-q^{*}(X))V_{01}^{*}(X)+q^{*}(X)V_{00}^{*}(X)}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})^{\top}\right]\in\real^{p\times p} \displaystyle A_{\mu\phi} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(1-q^{*}(X))}{(1-q^{*}(X))V_{01}^{*}(X)+q^{*}(X)V_{00}^{*}(X)}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})^{\top}\right]\in\real^{p\times q} \displaystyle A_{\phi\phi} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(1-q^{*}(X))}{(1-q^{*}(X))V_{01}^{*}(X)+q^{*}(X)V_{00}^{*}(X)}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})^{\top}\right]\in\real^{q\times q} \displaystyle b_{\mu} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-e^{*}(X))\mathcal{J}_{1}(X;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})}{(1-e^{*}(X))V_{11}^{*}(X)+e^{*}(X)V_{10}^{*}(X)}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})\right] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-q^{*}(X))\mathcal{J}_{0}(X;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})}{(1-q^{*}(X))V_{01}^{*}(X)+q^{*}(X)V_{00}^{*}(X)}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})\right]\in\real^{p} \displaystyle b_{\phi} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-q^{*}(X))\mathcal{J}_{0}(X;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})}{(1-q^{*}(X))V_{01}^{*}(X)+q^{*}(X)V_{00}^{*}(X)}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})\right]\in\real^{q}. $$

Taking $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}$ to give a more explicit EIF for $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , we can easily compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{0}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}) \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{1}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{1-\rho^{*}}\left(V_{11}^{*}(x)+\frac{e^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}V_{10}^{*}(x)\right). $$

Then some of the other expressions simplify:

$$ \displaystyle b_{\phi} \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle b_{\mu} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1-p^{*}(X)}{1-\rho^{*}}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})\right]=\mathbb{E}[D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})\mid S=0] \displaystyle\Gamma_{0}^{*}(x) \displaystyle=(1-q^{*}(x))\left(\frac{\Lambda_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+\Lambda_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})}{(1-q^{*}(x))V_{01}^{*}(x)+q^{*}(x)V_{00}^{*}(x)}\right) \displaystyle\Gamma_{1}^{*}(x) \displaystyle=(1-e^{*}(x))\left(\frac{\Lambda_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})}{(1-e^{*}(x))V_{11}^{*}(x)+e^{*}(x)V_{10}^{*}(x)}\right)+\frac{(1-p^{*}(x))}{(1-\rho^{*})p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)}. $$

Solving the matrix equations for the Lagrange multipliers then gives

$$ \displaystyle\Lambda_{1} \displaystyle=-\left(A_{\mu\mu}-A_{\mu\phi}A_{\phi\phi}^{-1}A_{\mu\phi}^{\top}\right)^{-1}b_{\mu}, \displaystyle\Lambda_{2}=-A_{\phi\phi}^{-1}A_{\mu\mu}^{\top}\Lambda_{1} \displaystyle=A_{\phi\phi}^{-1}A_{\mu\mu}^{\top}\left(A_{\mu\mu}-A_{\mu\phi}A_{\phi\phi}^{-1}A_{\mu\phi}^{\top}\right)^{-1}b_{\mu}. $$

Putting everything together, the EIF for $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{\textnormal{eff},\textnormal{obs}}^{(3)}(w;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}(w;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})- \displaystyle\quad\left(s\Gamma_{1}^{*}(x)+(1-s)\Gamma_{0}^{*}(x)\right)\left(z-(1-z)\left[\frac{se^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}+\frac{(1-s)q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}\right]\right)(y-m^{*}(r)) \displaystyle=\frac{1-s}{1-\rho^{*}}(m_{11}^{*}(x)-m_{10}^{*}(x)-\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*})+s\Delta(z,x,y;\eta^{*})\left(\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-\rho^{*})}-e^{*}(x)\Gamma_{1}^{*}(x)\right) \displaystyle\quad-(1-s)\Gamma_{0}^{*}(x)\left(z-(1-z)\frac{q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}\right)(y-m^{*}(r)) $$

where $\Gamma_{0}^{*}$ and $\Gamma_{1}^{*}$ are given by (67) and (68), respectively, for $\Lambda_{1}$ and $\Lambda_{2}$ as in (69) and (70).

We can now verify this matches the result in Theorem 4 of Yang et al. (2024). While that Theorem is stated as giving the efficient score of $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ rather than the efficient influence function of $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , this is incorrect according to S. Yang (personal communication, April 19, 2025). We correct the theorem below; essentially we must replace the efficient score $s_{\beta}(w;\eta^{*})$ for $\beta$ with the efficient influence function $\varphi_{\beta}(w;\eta^{*})$ for $\beta$ .

#### Theorem (Theorem 4, Yang et al. (2024), corrected).

Suppose Assumptions 1-3 hold. Then the EIF of $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ at the truth $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*}$ is

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:yang_{e}if}\tilde{\varphi}_{\textnormal{eff},\textnormal{obs}}^{(3)}(w;\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*},\eta^{*})=\frac{1-s}{1-\rho^{*}}(m_{11}^{*}(x)-m_{10}^{*}(x)-\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*})+\mathbb{E}\left[D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})^{\top}\mid S=0\right]\varphi_{\beta}(w;\eta^{*}) $$

where $\varphi_{\beta}(w;\eta^{*})$ is the first $p$ components of

$$ \varphi_{\lambda}(w;\eta^{*})=\left(\mathbb{E}\left[s_{\lambda}(W;\eta^{*})s_{\lambda}(W;\eta^{*})^{\top}\right]\right)^{-1}s_{\lambda}(w;\eta^{*}) $$

for

$$ \displaystyle s_{\lambda}(w;\eta^{*}) \displaystyle=(Z-\mathbb{E}[Z\omega^{*}(R)\mid S,X]\mathbb{E}[\omega^{*}(R)\mid S,X]^{-1})\omega^{*}(R)(Y-m^{*}(R))\begin{bmatrix}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})\\
D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})\end{bmatrix}, \displaystyle\omega^{*}(r) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{V^{*}(r)} $$

the efficient score for $\lambda=(\beta,\theta)$ , as given explicitly by Theorem 1 of Yang et al. (2024).

Showing that $\varphi_{\textnormal{eff},\textnormal{obs}}^{(3)}=\tilde{\varphi}_{\textnormal{eff},\textnormal{obs}}^{(3)}$ requires some algebra which we outline below. First we compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\omega^{*}(R)\mid S,X] \displaystyle=S\left(\frac{e^{*}(X)}{V_{11}^{*}(X)}+\frac{1-e^{*}(X)}{V_{10}^{*}(X)}\right)+(1-S)\left(\frac{q^{*}(X)}{V_{01}^{*}(X)}+\frac{1-q^{*}(X)}{V_{00}^{*}(X)}\right),\quad\text{ and } \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Z\omega^{*}(R)\mid S,X] \displaystyle=S\left(\frac{e^{*}(X)}{V_{11}^{*}(X)}\right)+(1-S)\left(\frac{q^{*}(X)}{V_{01}^{*}(X)}\right). $$

Then

### B.4 Linear confounding bias

Here we derive the EIF for an arbitrary scalar estimand $\tau$ , which can be estimated by an RAL estimator with influence function $\varphi_{0}$ , in the linear confounding bias model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}$ .

As argued in the main text, $\mathcal{M}_{4}$ is a linear space so $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}=\mathcal{M}_{4}$ by Proposition 2. The remainder of the EIF derivation closely follows the outcome-mediated selection bias example in Section 2.3. As in that example, we note $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}^{\perp}$ is precisely set of all functions $f\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ for which the projection $g=\Pi(f;\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}})$ is zero. Given $f$ , by the form of $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}=\mathcal{M}_{4}$ we can write

$$ g(r)=s(1-z)g_{1}(x)+(1-s)zg_{2}(x)+(1-s)(1-z)g_{3}(x)+sz\kappa(x;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}) $$

where $g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}$ in $\mathcal{H}_{X}$ and $\beta\in\real^{q}$ minimize the objective

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{O}(g_{1},g_{2},g_{3},\beta) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(f(R)-S(1-Z)g_{1}(X)-(1-S)Zg_{2}(X)-(1-S)(1-Z)g_{3}(X)-SZ\kappa(X;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3})\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(f_{11}(X)-\kappa(X;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}))^{2}+p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))(f_{10}(X)-g_{1}(X))^{2}] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))r^{*}(X)(f_{01}(X)-g_{2}(X))^{2}+(1-p^{*}(X))(1-r^{*}(X))(f_{00}(X)-g_{3}(X))^{2}] $$

over $\mathcal{H}_{X}^{3}\times\real^{q}$ , for

$$ \kappa(x;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3})=g_{1}(x)+g_{2}(x)-g_{3}(x)+\psi(x)^{\top}\beta. $$

The second equality follows from writing

$$ f(R)=SZf_{11}(X)+S(1-Z)f_{10}(X)+(1-S)Zf_{01}(X)+(1-S)(1-Z)f_{00}(X) $$

and conditioning on $X$ . With the objective now an expectation of a function of $X$ , for fixed $\beta$ we can minimize over $g_{1}$ , $g_{2}$ , and $g_{3}$ pointwise to obtain the first-order conditions

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=-p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(f_{11}(x)-\kappa(x;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}))-p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))(f_{10}(x)-g_{1}(x)) \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=-p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(f_{11}(x)-\kappa(x;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}))-(1-p^{*}(x))r^{*}(x)(f_{01}(x)-g_{2}(x)) \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(f_{11}(x)-\kappa(x;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}))-(1-p^{*}(x))(1-r^{*}(x))(f_{00}(x)-g_{3}(x)) $$

$$ \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}^{\perp}=\{w\mapsto f(r)(y-m^{*}(r))\mid f\in\mathcal{H}_{R}\text{ satisfies~\eqref{eq:T_M_perp_1},~\eqref{eq:T_M_perp_2},~\eqref{eq:T_M_perp_3}, and \eqref{eq:T_M_perp_4}}. $$

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:T_{M}{}_{1}{}_{p}erp}\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}^{\perp}=\{w\mapsto h(r;\eta^{*})\nu(x)(y-m^{*}(r))\mid\nu\in\mathcal{H}_{X},\ \mathbb{E}[\nu(X)\psi(X)]=0\}. $$

### B.5 Known RCT propensity scores

We characterize the EIF $\tilde{\varphi}_{\textnormal{eff}}$ for any pathwise differentiable estimand $\tau\in\real$ in the model $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ in terms of the EIF $\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}$ for the analogous model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ where the RCT propensity score $e^{*}$ is unknown. Our result will work for any mean function collection $\mathcal{M}$ satisfying the conditions of Corollary 1.

It is easy to see that the space

$$ \tilde{\mathcal{U}}=\{w\mapsto sh(x)(z-e^{*}(x))\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\} $$

is orthogonal to $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ . Hence

$$ \tilde{\varphi}_{\textnormal{eff}}=\varphi_{0}-\Pi(\varphi_{0};\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp})=\varphi_{0}-\Pi(\varphi_{0};\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp})-\Pi(\varphi_{0};\tilde{\mathcal{U}})=\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}-\Pi(\varphi_{0};\tilde{\mathcal{U}}) $$

where as in the main text, $\varphi_{0}$ is the influence function of any initial RAL estimator. Thus it suffices to compute $\Pi(\varphi_{0};\tilde{\mathcal{U}})$ . By definition

$$ \Pi(\varphi_{0};\tilde{\mathcal{U}})(w)=s\nu^{*}(x)(z-e^{*}(x)) $$

where

$$ \nu^{*}=\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W)-Sh(X)(Z-e^{*}(X))\right)^{2}\right]. $$

As usual, we expand the right-hand side and condition on $X$ :

$$ \displaystyle\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W)-Sh(X)(Z-e^{*}(X))\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\quad=\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}[S(Z-e^{*}(X))^{2}\mid X]h(X)^{2}-2\mathbb{E}[S(Z-e^{*}(X))\varphi_{0}(W)\mid X]h(X)\right] $$

We compute

$$ \mathbb{E}[S(Z-e^{*}(X))^{2}\mid X]=p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X)) $$

and so by minimizing pointwise we conclude

$$ \nu^{*}(x)=\frac{\mathbb{E}[S(Z-e^{*}(X))\varphi_{0}(W)\mid X=x]}{p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}. $$

For $\varphi_{0}\in\{\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}},\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}},\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}}\}$ we have

$$ \mathbb{E}[S(Z-e^{*}(X))\varphi_{0}(W)\mid X]=0 $$

and hence $\nu^{*}(x)=0$ . Thus, knowing the RCT propensity score does not improve the semiparametric efficiency bound for estimating $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ , $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , or $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ in any semiparametric model restricting the outcome mean function. In particular, the EIF’s $\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(k)},k=1,2,3,4,5$ in the models $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}$ for these estimands are also the EIF’s in the corresponding models $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}$ .

## Appendix C Conditions for efficiency

In this section, we provide specific primitive conditions under which the cross-fit one-step estimators $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}$ and $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}$ defined in Section 4 indeed attain the efficiency bound, by proving that these conditions imply those of the generalized Lemma in Section A.5. One condition is the following overlap assumption; a version of overlap is needed to even identify causal estimands in the nonparametric model.

#### Assumption 3 (Overlap).

There exists $\delta>0$ such that $e^{*}(x)\in[\delta,1-\delta]$ whenever $p^{*}(x)>0$ , $r^{*}(x)\in[\delta,1-\delta]$ , and $p^{*}(x)\in\{0\}\cup[\delta,1-\delta]$ for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ .

#### Remark 1.

The condition on $p^{*}(x)$ in Assumption 3 presumes that the support of the covariates in the RCT is contained within the support of the covariates of the observational dataset. Unlike typical analyses, we allow this inclusion to be strict since assumptions like linear confounding bias or outcome mediated selection permit extrapolation of the CATE beyond the support of the covariates in the RCT.

We also need the nuisance estimates to satisfy a similar overlap condition, as well as $o_{p}(N^{-1/4})$ root-mean-square convergence rates, typical in the double machine learning literature.

#### Assumption 4.

Cross-fit estimates of the nuisance functions $e^{*}$ , $m_{10}^{*}$ , $m_{01}^{*}$ , $m_{00}^{*}$ , $r^{*}$ , and $p^{*}$ satisfy Assumption 3 along with the following for each $k=1,\ldots,K$ :

- • (Convergence of infinite-dimensional nuisance estimates) $\displaystyle\|\hat{e}^{(-k)}-e^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{m}_{sz}^{(-k)}-m_{sz}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{r}^{(-k)}-r^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{p}^{(-k)}-p^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}$ (80) $\displaystyle\quad=o_{p}(N^{-1/4}),\quad(s,z)\neq(1,1)$ (81)

- • (Overlap in infinite-dimensional nuisance estimates) With probability tending to 1 as $N\rightarrow\infty$ , the statement of Assumption 3 holds with $e^{*}$ , $r^{*}$ , and $p^{*}$ replaced by their estimates $\hat{e}^{(-k)}$ , $\hat{r}^{(-k)}$ , and $\hat{p}^{(-k)}$ , respectively.

## Appendix D Details of numerical simulations in Section 5

Here we specify the full data generating processes for the numerical simulations in Section 5.

For the simulations in Section 5, in the discrete scenario, we emulate the data generating process in Section 5 of Guo et al. (2022):

$$ \displaystyle X=(X_{1},X_{2}) \displaystyle\sim\textnormal{Bern}(0.5)\times\textnormal{Bern}(0.5) \displaystyle Z\mid X \displaystyle\sim\textnormal{Bern}(X_{1}-X_{2}) \displaystyle Y\mid X,Z \displaystyle\sim\textnormal{Bern}\left(\textnormal{expit}\left(-0.5+Z+(1-2Z)(X_{1}-X_{2})\right)\right). $$

For the continuous scenario, we have

$$ \displaystyle X=(X_{1},X_{2}) \displaystyle\sim\mathcal{\mathbb{U}}(-1,1)\times\mathcal{\mathbb{U}}(-1,1) \displaystyle Z\mid X \displaystyle\sim\textnormal{Bern}(X_{1}-X_{2}) \displaystyle Y\mid X,Z \displaystyle\sim\textnormal{Bern}\left(\textnormal{expit}\left(-0.5+Z+(1-2Z)(X_{1}-X_{2})+(1.5Z-1)X_{1}X_{2}\right)\right). $$

To generate the simulated observational dataset, we draw observations from these DGP’s with the selection process described in Section 5 until 3000 selected observations are obtained. Then additional observations from the above DGP’s are generated without selection to form the RCT.

## Appendix E Implementation detail for control variate estimator

As indicated in the main text, our implementation of the control variate estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ follows the guidance of Guo et al. (2022). In the discrete scenario simulation, the differences $\{OR_{1}(x)-OR_{0}(x)\mid x\in\{0,1\}^{2}\}$ are used as four control variates. In the continuous scenario simulation and the Spambase data example, we use the average of $\log(OR_{1}(x))-\log(OR_{0}(x))$ over 50 randomly chosen distinct values of the covariates $x$ in the combined RCT and observational datasets as a single control variate. As the odds ratios are determinstic transformations of the outcome mean function $m$ , we can estimate all of these control variates via deterministic transformations of an outcome mean function estimator $\hat{m}$ . We use the same model for $\hat{m}$ as the cross-fit outcome mean function estimates $\hat{m}^{(-k)}$ used for computing the baseline estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ (i.e. the +1/+2 estimator in the discrete simulation scenario, MARS in the continuous simulation scenario ) except that we refit the model to the entire dataset (i.e. avoiding cross-fitting) as cross-fitting is not known to improve estimation of mean functions at a single point.

We can write

$$ \hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}=\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}-\hat{\Gamma}\hat{\lambda} $$

where $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ is the initial baseline estimator (AIPW or AIPSW in all simulations and the data example), $\hat{\lambda}$ is the estimate of the control variate(s) viewed as a vector, and $\hat{\Gamma}$ is an estimate of the optimal adjustment factor $\textnormal{cov}(\hat{\lambda},\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}})\textnormal{cov}(\hat{\lambda})^{-1}$ . The same adjustment $\hat{\Gamma}$ is used for all Monte Carlo simulations in each simulation scenario. This adjustment is computed by calculating $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ and $\hat{\lambda}$ in each of $B=1000$ Monte Carlo replicates of the data-generating process of the scenario, independent of the Monte Carlo replicates from which we report results, and then extracting the appropriate components of the sample covariance matrix. Similarly, for the Spambase data example, we compute $\hat{\Gamma}$ using the sample covariance matrix of estimates $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ and $\hat{\lambda}$ computed on $B=1000$ bootstrapped replications of the dataset, independent of the bootstrap replications on which we report results. This is exactly what is done by Guo et al. (2022). We remark that in practice, an investigator will not have access to additional, independent data on which to compute a regression adjustment independently of the data, and even if they did, they would want to use it for causal estimation to gain full efficiency. Thus, we believe a more accurate estimate of the performance of $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ would be reflected by computing a different adjustment factor $\hat{\Gamma}$ each time $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ is computed. We presume this is not done in Guo et al. (2022) due to the computation time required (each computation of $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ requires estimating nuisance functions, so estimating separate adjustments $\hat{\Gamma}$ would require fitting $B$ times as many nuisance function estimates).
